'''Francis Leslie Scott''' [[member of the Royal Irish Academy|MRIA]] (3 July 1928 – 14 January 2008) was an Irish [[chemist]] in the field of [[organic chemistry]], though he contributed equally to the wider scientific world.<ref name="UCC Memorial">{{cite web |url=https://www.rsc.org/events/detail/2690/memorial-evening-for-prof-francis-leslie-scott |title=Memorial Evening for Prof Francis Leslie Scott |last=Scott |first=Memorial |date=30 April 2009 |website=RSC |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry 2022 |access-date=20 October 2022 |quote=University College Cork, Ireland}}</ref>

Scott began his career at [[University College Cork]], where he published twenty-eight internationally refereed papers on organonitrogen chemistry, including several in the prestigious international journals [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']], the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'', ''[[The Journal of Organic Chemistry]]'' and ''[[Angewandte Chemie]]''. He published over 100 papers during his period as professor of chemistry at UCC.<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography">{{cite news |last=daughter |first=Scott |date=1 February 2022 |title= Scott, Francis Leslie ('Les') |url=https://www.dib.ie/biography/scott-francis-leslie-les-a10245 |work=Dictionary of Irish Biography |location=Ireland |access-date=20 October 2022}}</ref>

Many of Scott's students were critical to staffing Ireland's [[Regional Technical Colleges]]. Only ten percent left Ireland on a permanent basis, following Scott's hope of attracting top students and training them in the initial stage to keep them highly motivated.<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

==Education==
From 1945, Scott attended [[University College Cork]] first as an undergraduate, having gained first place in Ireland in both mathematics and chemistry. He completed an MSc in chemistry in 1948, graduating top of his class; in 1952, he completed a PhD on oxyiminotriazines with Professor Joseph Reilly. From 1949 to 1953 and alongside Joseph Reilly, Scott co-supervised twenty-five MSc and PhD students, including physicist Margaret Kennedy, whom he subsequently married.<ref name="UCC Memorial"/><ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

Scott obtained a university entrance scholarship to [[National University of Ireland]] (NUI).<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

==Career==
In 1953, Scott moved to the [[University of California]] (UCLA) in Los Angeles,<ref name="Chemistry Tree"/> where he continued research with the Canadian chemist [[Saul Winstein]]. In 1954, he began working for the Pennwalt Corporation in its research division, where he examined [[rocket propellant]]s and [[organic polymers]], finishing after 6 six years in 1960;<ref name="Chemistry Tree">{{cite web |url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=757221 |title=Francis Leslie Scott |last=Scott |first=Francis |date=12 June 2018 |website=Chemistry Tree |publisher=The Academic Family Tree |access-date=20 October 2022 |quote=1957–1960 Pennsalt Corporation}}</ref> his work was highly secretive. In 1955 he was appointed a lecturer in [[organic chemistry]] at UCLA, though he continued his independent research throughout. In 1958 at the age of 30, he earned a higher doctorate (D.Sc.), the youngest NUI graduate ever to do so.<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

In 1960, Scott succeeded Joseph Reilly as professor of chemistry at UCC. His professorship led to significant expansion in student numbers and research publications. His research was focused mostly on the fundamental mechanisms of chemical processes, including the study of high [[nitrogen]] compounds, [[Heterocyclic compound]]s and [[Organophosphorus compound|organophosphorus]] species. His publications covered many areas including neighbouring group effects, [[reactive intermediate]]s, [[sulfamic acid]]s and [[halogenation]]. In 1963 he was elected a [[member of the Royal Irish Academy]].<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

Scott was active in the UCC Graduates Association. Following a campaign on his behalf, he became a member of University College Cork's governing board from 1967 to 1973. During this time, he helped to fund many key physical developments. Scott was pivotal in the appointment of professors Joe Cunningham (of [[physical chemistry]]) and Brian Hathaway (of [[inorganic chemistry]]). He taught not only in his own field of organic chemistry, but also in the wider scientific world.<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

In the Cork area, Scott ran a series of major international conferences. The first, sponsored by [[The Royal Society of Chemistry]] in July 1964, was on [[organic reaction mechanisms]]; it attracted over 600 international devotees of industry and academia. Later conferences held were on inorganic [[reaction mechanism]], [[nitrogen|nitrogen chemistry]] and [[Sulfur|sulfur chemistry]]. This series of conferences ensured international attention for UCC chemistry.<ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>

After the death of his wife in 1973, Scott returned to University College Cork to work with [[Donald J. Cram]], who was later awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]].<ref name="UCC Memorial"/><ref name="Dictionary of Irish Biography"/>
